title: Orchard Well Depth and Drilling Costs
meta_description: Orchard wells have a 93 ft median depth, with finished-well costs commonly estimated at $10,600-$18,500.
h1: What Orchard, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
For rural property around Orchard, the local well records point to relatively shallow wells with strong reported production. Among permitted wells within five miles, the median reported depth is 93 feet, and the median reported yield is 34.0 gallons per minute. That is a useful starting point, but it is not a guarantee for a particular parcel.

The records also show a large mix of domestic, stock, irrigation and monitoring wells. Before buying land or pricing a new build, match the nearby well records to the parcel, confirm the intended use with Colorado DWR, and have a driller evaluate access, geology and the proposed well location.

sections.heading: Orchard well depths: shallow on average, but not uniform
sections.html:
Orchard’s recorded wells are much shallower than many mountain or fractured-granite areas. The median total depth is 93 feet, with the middle half running from 53 to 160 feet. About 53% are under 100 feet, while 46% fall between 100 and 300 feet. No recorded wells in this set fall between 300 and 600 feet or above 600 feet, although the deepest record reaches 1,430 feet.

For a drilling bid, the middle-half range is more useful than the median alone. A site near 160 feet can cost substantially more than one near 53 feet. Ground conditions, the target aquifer, casing and grout requirements, and the water right or permit limitations all affect the final design.

sections.heading: Reported yields are strong, but confirm the well type
sections.html:
Only 151 wells report a pump yield, so the yield statistics do not describe every permitted well. Among those reports, the median is 34.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half ranges from 15.0 to 1,200.0 gallons per minute. The records show 93% producing more than 15 gallons per minute, with no reported wells under 1 gallon per minute.

That is encouraging for Orchard, but do not treat a high irrigation-well result as a promise for a household well. Use, construction, testing method and aquifer all matter. A domestic well may need only modest flow, while irrigation can require a much larger supply. Have the driller perform and document an appropriate pump test.

sections.heading: Orchard water levels and the change in recent records
sections.html:
Static water level is reported for only 60 wells. The overall median depth to water is 36 feet, with the middle half from 11 to 54 feet below the surface. That gives a buyer a practical expectation for pumping equipment and trench planning, but the actual level can vary by location, season, pumping nearby wells and measurement conditions.

The decade figures deserve attention. The median reported water level was 14 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 43 feet in the 2020s. That indicates deeper measured water levels in the newer group of records. It is not, by itself, proof of a basin-wide decline, because the wells and measurement locations may differ.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Orchard, and how old are the records
sections.html:
Orchard has a long permit history. The records include 45 permits from the 1950s, 59 from the 1960s, 57 from the 1970s, 38 from the 1980s, 87 from the 1990s, 100 from the 2000s, 110 from the 2010s and 81 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 95 wells, Canfield, Leslie George with 93, and Canfield Drilling Company (Canfield, Harold E) with 58. These names help with local research, but they do not replace a current bid or a site-specific evaluation. Ask for references and verify current licensing before hiring.

sections.heading: What a new Orchard well may cost
sections.html:
For Orchard’s Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, the drilling rate model is $50-$70 per foot. Applying that range to the 93-foot median depth produces an estimated drilled-hole cost of about $4,600-$6,500. That is only the hole. It does not represent the complete water system or every permit and site expense.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at approximately $10,600-$18,500 at the median depth. A deeper-than-median site, difficult access, extra casing, long utility runs or special treatment can move the price higher. Get a written scope that separates drilling, casing, grout, pump equipment, testing, electrical and trenching.

sections.heading: Orchard risks: water quality, permits and the building site
sections.html:
The mapped area has 60 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles. There are no historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the mapped data. That does not establish the quality of an individual well. Test existing water and plan testing for a new well, especially if the property is close to a mapped site or has an uncertain land-use history.

Permits show a mix of domestic or household use at 33%, stock at 18%, irrigation at 33% and monitoring at 19%. Confirm that the permit fits your intended use. Colorado exempt household-use wells have a 35 gallon-per-minute pumping limit, and augmentation plans may matter in over-appropriated basins. Keep the well, septic system and building site separated as required by current rules.

sections.heading: What to do before buying or building near Orchard
sections.html:
Start with neighboring wells, not a countywide average. Records near Jackson Lake, Wiggins, Weldona, Trail Side, Morgan Heights and Log Lane Village can provide useful regional context, but the closest comparable wells are the most valuable. Compare construction dates, depths, aquifer names, reported yields and static water levels, then have a Colorado well professional review the actual permit files.

For a vacant lot, make the well location, septic area, driveway access and house footprint work together before closing. Confirm DWR permitting, water use, electrical access and drilling access. For an existing home, collect a recent water-quality report, pump information and maintenance history. A strong nearby yield is helpful; it is not a substitute for testing and a site-specific well plan.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Orchard, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Orchard is 93 feet. The middle half runs from 53 to 160 feet, with 53% under 100 feet and 46% between 100 and 300 feet. One record reaches 1,430 feet, so local variation still matters when estimating a new well.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Orchard?
faq.a: The drilling model for Orchard is $50-$70 per foot. At the 93-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $4,600-$6,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $10,600-$18,500. A driller should price the actual site and intended use.

faq.q: How much water do Orchard wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 151 wells that report pump yield, the median is 34.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 1,200.0 gallons per minute, and 93% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Those figures include different well uses, so a household buyer should verify the specific well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Orchard?
faq.a: The records do not establish that every Orchard well is safe to drink. There are 60 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, so testing is important. Request recent results for an existing home and test a new well for relevant contaminants before relying on it for household use.

faq.q: Are Orchard well water levels getting lower?
faq.a: The median reported static water level was 14 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 43 feet in the 2020s. That shows deeper measurements in the newer decade group, but it does not prove a basin-wide decline because the wells, locations and measurement conditions may differ. Review nearby records before buying.
